title: Thinking and Working Scientifically: Models, Investigations and Analysing Results
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Science 0893 · Stage 8 · Start here
summary: Every Stage 8 science skill — analogies and formulae, hypotheses, planning, risk, keys, accurate measuring, tables, graphs, anomalies, conclusions and evaluation — with one investigation followed from start to finish.

blocks.text: Thinking and Working Scientifically (TWS) is how scientists ask questions, plan, measure, and decide what their results mean. In tests it is mixed into almost every question, so these skills earn marks in biology, chemistry, physics, and Earth and space. On this page one investigation — **how the number of coils changes the strength of an electromagnet** — runs through most of the sections, so you can see every step of real science.

blocks.text: 1. Models: analogies, symbols and formulae

An **analogy** is a comparison between something new and difficult and something familiar that works in a **similar way**. Scientists use analogies as **models**: they help us understand, explain and even predict. But an analogy is never exactly the same as the real thing, so every analogy has **limitations** (ways it does not match).

rows: Shows that the heart pushes blood round the body.
The heart is a living muscle that beats by itself.
water flowing in pipes, pushed by a pump
Cell = pump, wires = pipes, current = flow of water; a narrow pipe is like a resistance.
Water spills from a broken pipe; current does not pour out of a cut wire.
A small, heavy centre (nucleus) with electrons around it, like planets round the Sun.
Electrons are held by electric attraction, not gravity; most of the atom is empty space.
two people pulling a door with ropes from opposite sides
Each one can only pull, so you need one on each side to open and to close it.
Muscles are joined to bones by tendons and change shape when they contract.

blocks.text: **Using an analogy for a purpose (8TWSm.02):** choose the part of the analogy that matches the question. For example: "Use the pipe analogy to explain why adding a second cell makes a bigger current." → A second pump pushes the water harder, so more water flows each second; in the same way two cells push a bigger current round the circuit.
**Symbols and formulae (8TWSm.03)** are another kind of model: short, exact ways to write scientific ideas that everyone in the world understands.

headers: Examples you will use in Stage 8
rows: O_{2} (oxygen), CO_{2} (carbon dioxide), H_{2}O (water), Fe (iron), Mg (magnesium), NaCl (sodium chloride)
speed = distance ÷ time; pressure = force ÷ area; moment = force × distance
m (metre), s (second), m/s (metres per second), N (newton), cm³ (cubic centimetre), °C, g, kg
circuit symbols for a cell, lamp, switch; arrows for forces and for rays of light

blocks.text: 2. Hypotheses and predictions

A **hypothesis** is a scientific idea that explains something, for example: "An electromagnet with more coils of wire is stronger, because more turns of current make a stronger magnetic field." A **prediction** says what you expect to happen in your investigation, and **why**, using science you know: "I predict that if I double the number of coils, the electromagnet will pick up about twice as many paperclips, because…"

**Is it testable? (8TWSp.01)** A hypothesis is testable only if you can collect evidence about it by observing or measuring. Opinions (best, prettiest, nicest, more fun) and ideas about things that cannot be measured are **not** testable.

rows: Plants grow taller in more light.
You can change the light and measure the height.
Iron rusts faster in salty water.
You can compare the rust on nails in salty and in pure water.
Gold is the most beautiful metal.
"Beautiful" is an opinion; it cannot be measured.
People will live on Mars in the year 3000.

blocks.text: **Evidence supports or contradicts (8TWSp.02).** If the results match the prediction, the evidence **supports** the hypothesis. If they do not, the evidence **contradicts** it, and the hypothesis may need to change. One investigation never **proves** a hypothesis for ever: other scientists repeat the work, and new evidence can still change our ideas.
3. Planning investigations
In a **fair test** you change **one** variable, measure **one** variable and keep **all the others the same**.

rows: The one you change on purpose
Ones you keep the same, so the test is fair
same iron nail (core), same wire, same battery/voltage, same size of paperclips

blocks.text: **Not all investigations can be fair tests (8TWSp.04).** Scientists choose the type of enquiry that fits the question:

rows: You can change one variable and control the rest.
Does the number of coils affect the strength of an electromagnet?
You cannot control the variables, so you collect lots of data and look for a pattern.
Do people who smoke have more breathing problems?
How does the Moon's shape change over a month?
You sort things into groups or name them.
Using a key to identify invertebrates in a pond.
The investigation is too big, slow or dangerous to do yourself.
How has the Earth's climate changed over 800 000 years?
The real thing is too small, big or far away.
Using a ball-and-string model to explain how a hinge joint moves.

blocks.text: **Choosing equipment (8TWSc.02).** Choose an instrument that measures the right quantity, with a suitable **range** (big enough) and fine enough **scale divisions**.

rows: measuring cylinder (small volumes: syringe or pipette)
gas syringe, or upturned measuring cylinder in water

blocks.text: 4. Risk assessments and working safely

A **hazard** is something that could cause harm (acid, a flame, hot water). The **risk** is the chance that harm happens. A **risk assessment** lists the hazards and how you will **control** (reduce) the risk. Then you follow it while you work (8TWSp.05, 8TWSc.05).

rows: Wire of an electromagnet gets hot
use a low voltage; switch off between readings; do not hold the coil
wear eye protection (goggles); wipe up spills; wash skin with water
burns; hair or paper catches fire
tie back hair; heatproof mat; keep paper away; use the safety (yellow) flame when not heating
let it cool; use tongs; stand up while heating
tell the teacher; do not pick up with fingers

blocks.text: 5. Sorting, classifying and keys

Scientists **sort and classify** objects, materials and living things by **testing** (is it magnetic? does it conduct electricity?), by **observation** (number of legs, leaf shape), by **secondary information** (books, databases) and by using **keys** (8TWSc.01). A **dichotomous key** asks one question at a time with two possible answers (yes/no), until only one thing is left.

blocks.text: **Using the key:** a leaf is not divided into leaflets and has smooth edges: no → no → **B**. A leaf has 7 leaflets: yes → yes → **C**. **Making a key:** choose features you can see clearly and that split the group into two ("Has it got legs?"), never opinions ("Is it big?" — big compared with what?).
6. Accuracy, precision and repeating measurements

**Accurate** measurements are close to the **true value**. **Precise** measurements are close to **each other** when you repeat them; a precise instrument has small scale divisions (a thermometer marked every 0.5 °C is more precise than one marked every 2 °C). Accuracy and precision matter because conclusions are only as good as the measurements they are based on (8TWSc.04).

blocks.text: How to measure accurately: read scales at **eye level**; read a liquid at the **bottom of the meniscus**; check the balance reads zero before you start; choose an instrument with a suitable scale; start the stopwatch and stop it at exactly the right moments.

blocks.text: **Repeating (8TWSc.03).** Repeat each measurement (often three times) and calculate a **mean**. Repeats let you spot anomalous results. Your readings are **repeated sufficiently** (enough) if the repeats are **close together**. If they are spread out, do more repeats.

**Secondary sources (8TWSc.06).** Information from books, websites, adverts and other people's results must be checked. Is it **relevant** (about exactly your question)? Is it from a **reliable** source (scientists, a university, an official organisation)? Could it be **biased** — written by someone who gains from you believing it, such as a company selling a product? Compare several sources.
7. Recording results

Collect **enough** results (at least five different values of the independent variable, with repeats) and record them in a table as you go (8TWSc.07). Rules: independent variable in the **first column**; dependent variable in the next columns; **units in the headings**, not in every box; same number of decimal places in a column.

In the row for 40 coils, trial 2 (7) is far from the other two (12 and 12): it is **anomalous**, so it is left out of the mean. Mean = (12 + 12) ÷ 2 = 12. A possible cause: some paperclips fell off, or the current was not switched on fully.
8. Presenting results: bar chart or line graph?

rows: **categoric** — names or groups (types of metal, kinds of food)
volume of gas made by different metals in acid
**continuous** — numbers that can take any value (time, temperature, length, number of coils)
paperclips picked up for different numbers of coils

blocks.text: 9. Trends, anomalies, conclusions and evaluation

**Describe the trend (8TWSa.02):** use the sentence "As the [independent variable] increases, the [dependent variable] increases / decreases", then add numbers. From the graph: "As the number of coils increases from 10 to 60, the number of paperclips increases from 3 to 18. The paperclips increase by 3 for every 10 extra coils (a straight line through the origin)." The point at 40 coils (8 paperclips) is **anomalous**: it is well below the line.

**Was the prediction accurate? (8TWSa.01)** Compare the prediction with the results and give a reason. "I predicted that doubling the coils would double the paperclips. My prediction was accurate: 20 coils picked up 6 paperclips and 40 coils picked up 12 (mean values)." If a prediction was not accurate, suggest why — perhaps your scientific idea was incomplete, or there was an error in the measurements.

**Conclusion and its limitations (8TWSa.03):** a conclusion says what the results show, using the evidence: "The more coils, the stronger the electromagnet." **Limitations** are the limits of what you can claim: it was only tested from 10 to 60 coils, with one type of nail and one battery; paperclips only measure strength roughly (you cannot pick up half a paperclip).

**Evaluate and improve (8TWSa.04):** say what went well or badly in the method and suggest a change **with a reason**. Example: "Use smaller paperclips or measure the force with a newton meter, so the strength can be measured more precisely." "Repeat each reading three times and calculate a mean, so anomalous results can be spotted and the results are more reliable." "Use a variable resistor and ammeter to keep the current the same, so that it is a fair test."

blocks.title: المتغيرات في سطرين
blocks.text: المتغيّر المستقل = اللي إنت بتغيّره بإيدك. المتغيّر التابع = اللي بتقيسه. المتغيّرات الثابتة = كل حاجة تانية لازم تفضل زي ما هي عشان التجربة تبقى عادلة (fair test). ولو فيه نتيجة بعيدة عن الباقي (anomalous) متدخلهاش في حساب المتوسط.
Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — using an analogy
A teacher says: "An electric circuit is like water flowing round a loop of pipes, pushed by a pump."
(a) What is an analogy? [1] (b) In this analogy, what does the pump represent? [1] (c) Give one limitation of this analogy. [1]

items: (a) A comparison with something familiar that works in a similar way, used to help explain a scientific idea.
(b) The **cell** (or battery) — it pushes the current round, as the pump pushes the water.
(c) If a pipe breaks, water pours out, but if a wire is cut the electric current does not flow out — it just stops. (Accept other sensible differences.)

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** in (c), saying what is the **same**. A limitation is a way the analogy is **different** from the real thing.

**Worked example 2** — testable hypotheses and evidence
Omar's hypothesis: "Seeds germinate faster when they are warmer." (a) Is this hypothesis testable? Explain your answer. [1] (b) Seeds at 25 °C germinated in 3 days; seeds at 10 °C took 8 days. Does this evidence support or contradict the hypothesis? [1]

items: (a) Yes: he can change the temperature and **measure** the time the seeds take to germinate.
(b) It **supports** the hypothesis: the warmer seeds germinated faster (3 days compared with 8 days).
Note: say "supports", not "proves". More tests, at more temperatures and with more seeds, would make the evidence stronger.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 3** — planning
Laila investigates how the number of coils affects the strength of an electromagnet.
(a) Name the independent and dependent variables. [2] (b) Name two control variables. [2] (c) Write a prediction and give a scientific reason. [2]

items: (a) Independent: the **number of coils** [1]. Dependent: the **number of paperclips** picked up [1].
(b) Any two: the same nail (core); the same battery / voltage / current; the same type and size of paperclips; the same wire [2].
(c) Prediction: more coils will pick up more paperclips [1]. Reason: more turns of wire carrying current make a **stronger magnetic field** [1].

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** a prediction with no reason ("It will pick up more") scores only 1 of the 2 marks.

**Worked example 4** — repeats, means and anomalies
Use the results table in section 7. (a) Which result is anomalous? [1] (b) Calculate the mean for 20 coils. [1] (c) Have the readings been repeated enough? Explain. [1]

items: (a) 40 coils, trial 2 (7 paperclips) — far below 12 and 12.
(c) Yes: for each number of coils the three repeats are close together (within 1 or 2 paperclips), apart from one anomaly, which was easy to spot.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 5** — graphs and conclusions
Use Laila's graph. (a) Describe the trend. [2] (b) Use the line of best fit to predict the number of paperclips for 35 coils. [1] (c) State one limitation of her conclusion. [1]

items: (a) As the number of coils increases, the number of paperclips increases [1]; from 3 paperclips at 10 coils to 18 at 60 coils / it goes up in proportion (doubling the coils doubles the paperclips) [1].
(b) Go up from 35 on the x-axis to the line, then across: 0.3 × 35 = 10.5, so about **10 or 11** paperclips (you cannot pick up half a paperclip).
(c) It was only tested between 10 and 60 coils / with one size of nail / with one battery, so we do not know what happens outside these conditions.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 6** — choosing equipment and improving accuracy
Adam needs to measure 8 cm³ of water. He can choose a 10 cm³, a 100 cm³ or a 1000 cm³ measuring cylinder. (a) Which should he choose? Explain. [2] (b) Suggest how he should read the scale. [1]

items: (a) The **10 cm³** cylinder [1]: it has smaller scale divisions (e.g. 0.2 cm³), so the measurement is more precise/accurate; a large cylinder has big divisions and 8 cm³ would only fill the bottom [1].
(b) With his eye level with the **bottom of the meniscus**, on a flat surface.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up independent (changed) and dependent (measured) variables. Ask: "Which one did they choose before starting?"
Control variables written as "the amount" — name the quantity: "the volume of acid", "the mass of the magnesium".
Joining dot to dot on a line graph, or drawing a line of best fit through the anomalous point.
Including an anomalous result in the mean.
Saying results "prove" a hypothesis. Evidence supports or contradicts it.
Describing a trend with no numbers, or a prediction with no reason.
Using a bar chart for continuous data such as temperature or time.
Saying "repeat it to make it a fair test". Repeats make results more **reliable**; controlling variables makes it **fair**.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Name the independent variable / two variables that should be kept the same." [1] each — be specific.
"Which result is anomalous? Suggest a reason." Find the value that breaks the pattern; give a real experimental cause.
"Calculate the mean." Leave out the anomaly; show the sum and the division.
"Plot the results and draw a line of best fit." Plot crosses exactly; smooth line; ignore anomalies.
"Describe the pattern." As … increases, … increases/decreases + numbers.
"Was the prediction correct? Use the results." Yes/no + data from the table.
"Suggest one improvement and explain why." Change + reason (more accurate / more reliable / fairer).
"Which source is most reliable?" Think: who wrote it, and do they gain from it?

blocks.title: الدقة والتكرار
blocks.text: accurate يعني قريب من القيمة الحقيقية، و precise يعني القراءات المتكررة قريبة من بعض. بنكرر التجربة ٣ مرات ونحسب المتوسط عشان النتائج تبقى موثوقة (reliable). التكرار مش بيخلي التجربة عادلة — اللي بيخليها عادلة هو تثبيت المتغيرات.
Practice

blocks.title: Thinking and Working Scientifically: practice
blocks.intro: 14 Checkpoint-style questions on models, planning, measuring and analysing. Full solutions are shown after you check.

questions.q: Which statement best describes an analogy?
c: an exact, full-size copy of a real object
a comparison with something familiar that works in a similar way
a prediction of what will happen in an experiment
a list of the equipment needed
questions.e: An analogy explains something new by comparing it with something familiar that behaves in a similar way (e.g. the heart is like a pump). It is a model, so it is never an exact copy.

questions.q: Speed is written as a formula: speed = distance ÷ time. A toy car travels 3 m in 4 s. Calculate its speed.
Which hypothesis is testable by a scientific investigation?
c: Blue flowers are prettier than red flowers.
Science lessons are more fun in the morning.
Salt dissolves faster in warm water than in cold water.
Cats are better pets than dogs.
questions.e: Only the salt hypothesis can be checked by measuring something (the time to dissolve at different temperatures). The others are opinions: "prettier", "more fun" and "better" cannot be measured in a fair, agreed way.

questions.p:
Question 4
Karim adds a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. He measures the volume of gas made in 1 minute. He repeats this with acid of different concentrations.
questions.e: Karim changes the concentration of the acid on purpose, so it is the independent variable.

questions.p:
Question 4
Karim adds a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. He measures the volume of gas made in 1 minute. He repeats this with acid of different concentrations.
ans: volume of gas made in 1 minute
questions.e: He measures the volume of gas made in 1 minute — that is the dependent variable.

questions.p:
Question 4
Karim adds a 2 cm piece of magnesium ribbon to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid. He measures the volume of gas made in 1 minute. He repeats this with acid of different concentrations.
questions.q: (c) Name two control variables Karim must keep the same.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, any two: length / mass of magnesium ribbon (2 cm); volume of acid (25 cm³); temperature of the acid; time the gas is collected for (1 minute); type of acid (hydrochloric). Do not accept: concentration of the acid (independent variable); volume of gas (dependent variable); "the amount" with no quantity named.
questions.e: The question already tells you some: 2 cm of magnesium, 25 cm³ of acid, 1 minute. Temperature also changes the rate of reaction, so it must be kept the same.

questions.q: Hana wants to find out whether students with longer legs can run 100 m faster. What type of investigation is this, and why?
c: pattern seeking, because many other variables (fitness, age, practice) cannot be controlled
a fair test, because she can control every variable
observing over time, because she watches one student for a year
identifying and classifying, because she sorts students into groups
questions.e: She cannot change people's leg length or control their fitness, so it cannot be a fair test. She collects data from many students and looks for a pattern — pattern seeking.

questions.q: Read the volume of liquid in the measuring cylinder.
questions.e: Each small division is 1 cm³ (five spaces between 20 and 25). Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level: it is two divisions above 25, so 27 cm³.

questions.q: Four students time how long a sugar cube takes to dissolve. Their results are 24 s, 25 s, 31 s and 23 s. One result is anomalous. Calculate the mean of the other three results.
questions.e: 31 s is far from the others, so it is anomalous and is left out. Mean = (24 + 25 + 23) ÷ 3 = 72 ÷ 3 = 24 s. [1 mark for leaving out 31, 1 mark for 24]

questions.p:
Question 10
Rana counts the paperclips picked up by an electromagnet with different numbers of coils.
number of coils | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50
number of paperclips | 4 | 8 | 5 | 16 | 20
questions.q: Which number of coils gave the anomalous result?
questions.e: The pattern is 4 paperclips for every 10 coils: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20. At 30 coils we expect 12 but Rana got 5, so 30 coils is the anomalous result.

questions.q: Sara measures the temperature of a beaker of hot water every minute for 10 minutes as it cools. How should she present her results?
c: a bar chart
a pie chart
a pictogram
a line graph
questions.e: Both time and temperature are continuous (they can have any value), so a line graph is used. Bar charts are for categories (e.g. different metals).

questions.p:
Question 12
A student measures the mass of potassium nitrate that dissolves in 100 g of water at different temperatures.
temperature in °C | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80
mass that dissolves in g | 32 | 64 | 110 | 169
questions.q: Describe the pattern in the results. Use numbers in your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: as the temperature increases, the mass that dissolves increases (ora). 1 mark: correct use of data, e.g. from 32 g at 20 °C to 169 g at 80 °C; OR the mass increases by larger amounts as the temperature rises (32 g, then 46 g, then 59 g). Do not accept: "it increases" with no variable named.
questions.e: As the temperature increases from 20 °C to 80 °C, the mass of potassium nitrate that dissolves increases from 32 g to 169 g. The increase gets bigger at higher temperatures: +32 g, +46 g, +59 g for each 20 °C.

questions.q: A company says its new energy drink improves exam results. Which source of information is most likely to be biased?
c: an advert written by the company that sells the drink
a report by scientists who tested the drink on 500 students and have no link to the company
a school science textbook
a government health website
questions.e: The company makes money if people believe the drink works, so its advert may only show the good results — it is likely to be biased.

questions.q: Students heat water to 80 °C in a beaker over a Bunsen burner. Identify one hazard and describe how to control the risk.
questions.ms: 1 mark for a hazard: hot water / hot beaker or tripod can burn (scald); Bunsen flame can burn skin or set hair, ties or paper on fire; glass beaker can break. 1 mark for a matching control: let equipment cool before touching / use tongs; tie back long hair, tuck in ties, keep paper away; use a heatproof mat; stand up while heating; wear eye protection (goggles) in case of splashes. The control must match the hazard.
questions.e: Example: Hazard: the hot water and beaker can burn your skin. Control: do not touch the beaker until it has cooled, and move it with tongs; wear goggles in case the water spits.

blocks.title: Remember
items: An analogy compares a new idea with something familiar; always know one limitation.
Independent = changed, dependent = measured, control = kept the same. Not every investigation can be a fair test.
Accurate = close to the true value; precise = repeats close together. Repeat, leave out anomalies, calculate the mean.
Bar chart for categories; line graph for continuous data, with a line of best fit.
Describe trends with numbers; conclusions need evidence and limitations; improvements need a reason.
